body:
frume@yahoo.com posted:

>Excerpts from interviews with American dissident and
>media critic Noam Chomsky...

>Sources:  The Noam Chomsky Archive
>http://www.worldmedia.com/archive
>http://www.geocities.com/CapitolHill/Senate/3761/

I wrote:
>> I just hope that the public starts listening to the new simple lifestyle
>> bookwriters who, among other things, encourage people to stop watching the
>news
>> because it is too depressing.

Frume quoted:
>Interviewer:  You say that "people should tear away
>the masks of ideological distortion and indoctrination"
>... Maybe it's Hume's Paradox:  people have to give
>their consent to be ruled. But if they just withhold
>consent, saying, "you haven't convinced me," does that
>mean that the power structure goes away?
>
>Noam Chomsky: Well, if you just withhold consent
>privately at home, nothing happens. If withholding
>consent is a step toward organization and action, then a
>lot can change. In fact, you can claim that you
>are withholding consent and still be consenting to the
>structure. For example, suppose that you're
>living in a society that has slavery. If you sit at home
>quietly and say, "I object to slavery," that's
>giving your consent. ...
>
>Interviewer: ... Cannot the individual ignore the
>propaganda outpourings of the culture by turning off
>the TV and the radio and not reading the corporate
>press?
>
>Chomsky: Again we're back to consent. That's a form
>of consent.
>

Indeed, not buying into the corporate media is not active dissent, but it is a
first step in freeing one's mind. Once you allow yourself to think for
yourself, you are a step closer to the ability to act and give your consent as
you really see fit.

One of the other things those books I mentioned do is to show people how much
less complicated and happier their lives could be if they got off the
recreational shopping bandwagon, and were happy with what they already had,
both materially and in life in general. If enough people took heed to those
ideas, there would be serious changes in our growth oriented industrial
economy.
Furthurmore, these changes could be gradual enough that there would be no
bloodbath.

So, in a way, spreading this message is a small step on the road to action.

<snip - there was a lot here, and I think I would like to take it up later>

I wrote:
>> I don't know that the public is as stupid as the press and their "clients"
>take
>> us for. Often naive, but often frustrated too, at having words put into our
>> mouths that we would never have uttered. But if pushed hard enough, and if
>> enough people begin to question and doubt, that will give free thinkers the
>> upper hand, at least for a few moments, perhaps enough to seize the day.

Frume quoted:
>Interviewer: Does ownership always determine and
>drive content?
>
>Chomsky:  In some far-reaching sense it does. That is,
>if content ever goes beyond the bounds that ownership
>will tolerate, it will surely move in to limit it. On the
>other hand, that permits a fair amount of flexibility. So
>investors don't go down to the television studio and
>make sure that the local talk show host or news
>director is doing what they want. On the other hand,
>there are other complex mechanisms which make it
>fairly certain that they will do what the owners and
>investors want.  There's a whole filtering process that
>enables people to rise through the system into
>managerial roles only if they've demonstrated that
>they've successfully internalized the values demanded
>by private power.
>
>At that point they can describe themselves as quite
>free. So you'll occasionally find the sort of flaming
>independent liberal type. I remember columns by Tom
>Wicker saying, Look, nobody tells me what to say. I
>do anything I feel. It's an absolutely free system. And
>for him that's just right. After he had demonstrated to
>the satisfaction of the bosses that he had internalized
>their values, he was entirely free to write anything he
>wanted.
>

Yes, of course. One more example for the manifesto, which discusses this in the
"The Nature of Freedom" section,  paragraph 98, "One more point to be made in
this section: It should not be assumed that a person has enough freedom just
because he SAYS he has enough. Freedom is restricted in part by psychological 
control of which people are unconscious..." and in paragraph 94, "It is
important not to confuse freedom with mere permissiveness..."

My original point about NPR is that it seems to me a less corporate news
source. I don't think it is a panacea, but I do think that listening to
programs like theirs, (and other alternative news sources recently posted)
instead of the mainstream media, may shake a few more people out of their
complacency, instead of lulling them into believing that everything's going to
be alright.



SJJ
"Whoso wants to be a man must also be a non-conformist!" - Emerson
